Beyond software / Infrastructure case study

Home Lab & Infrastructure

Physical hardware, real workloads, and hands-on practice in Linux administration, networking, DNS, self-hosting, service reliability, and resource management.

Built at home. Operated with intent.

Two machines.
Distinct responsibilities.

A Debian server takes on the heavier workloads. A dedicated Raspberry Pi handles DNS and filtering. Together, they give me a practical place to understand how services behave, where connectivity breaks, and what keeps a workload running.

02 / Server operations

Debian 12. A working server.

I administer the server remotely over SSH, manage services and processes, and monitor CPU and memory while workloads run. Troubleshooting means following a problem from the running process through to its network connection.

03 / A real-world workload

Hosting Prominence II.

Multiplayer Minecraft server

A heavy multiplayer modpack gives the Debian server a real workload: balancing memory use and CPU load, managing the server process, troubleshooting connections, and keeping the service running. The playit.gg tunnel provides connectivity for players.

  • Resource limitsMemory allocation & CPU load
  • Service operationProcesses, troubleshooting & uptime
  • ConnectivityMultiplayer access through playit.gg

04 / Dedicated network services

Small machine. Clear responsibility.

The Raspberry Pi 4 runs Pi-hole for local DNS and domain filtering. I use SSH to administer it and trace DNS behavior when troubleshooting the network.

Keeping this lightweight infrastructure on its own device separates DNS and filtering from the heavier workloads on the Debian server.

  1. Raspberry Pi 4
  2. Pi-hole
  3. Local DNS / filtering

The real dashboard shows DNS activity, blocked queries, domains on blocklists, and client activity.

05 / How it connects

One network, distinct responsibilities.

Shared connectivity, separate jobs. The Debian server hosts workloads; the Raspberry Pi handles DNS and filtering.

06 / Engineering practice

What I learned.

Think in services
Manage persistent Linux services and their processes remotely through SSH, beyond a desktop session.
Trace connectivity problems
Distinguish DNS issues from network and service failures across real hardware and software.
Work within resource limits
Use CPU and memory monitoring to understand the constraints of a running server workload.
Separate responsibilities
Keep DNS and filtering on the Pi while the Debian server handles heavier workloads.

About

Hey, I'm Tim — a backend developer who enjoys building systems that solve real problems.

I have production experience with C#, ASP.NET, SQL Server, and Azure, along with backend development using Node.js and PostgreSQL. I currently work in enterprise IT at DART Aerospace.

When I have free time, I read books, listen to Hans Zimmer, build Python web apps, experimenting with APIs and automation, and trying new ideas that turn my problems into a project. I'm the kind of guy who genuinely enjoys learning and improving with every project. Also, I enjoy solving people's problems, so if you have any, feel free to reach out!
